claim: Centrioles are composed of long-lived microtubules arranged in nine triplets.
source: Centrioles are composed of long-lived microtubules arranged in nine triplets.
evidence: This is a statement of established knowledge about centriole structure, supported by citation to prior work (Kochanski and Borisy, 1990; Balestra et al., 2015) in the full text.

claim: The contribution of triplet microtubules to mammalian centriole formation and stability is unknown.
source: However, the contribution of triplet microtubules to mammalian centriole formation and stability is unknown.
evidence: This is a statement about the state of knowledge in the field at the time of the study.

claim: Delta-tubulin and epsilon-tubulin are required for triplet microtubule formation in unicellular eukaryotes.
source: Little is known of the mechanism of triplet microtubule formation, but experiments in unicellular eukaryotes indicate that delta-tubulin and epsilon-tubulin, two less-studied tubulin family members, are required.
evidence: This claim is supported by references to prior experimental work in unicellular organisms.

claim: Centrioles in delta-tubulin null mutant human cells lack triplet microtubules.
source: Here, we report that centrioles in delta-tubulin and epsilon-tubulin null mutant human cells lack triplet microtubules and fail to undergo centriole maturation.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by electron microscopy data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Centrioles in epsilon-tubulin null mutant human cells lack triplet microtubules.
source: Here, we report that centrioles in delta-tubulin and epsilon-tubulin null mutant human cells lack triplet microtubules and fail to undergo centriole maturation.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by electron microscopy data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Centrioles in delta-tubulin null mutant human cells fail to undergo centriole maturation.
source: Here, we report that centrioles in delta-tubulin and epsilon-tubulin null mutant human cells lack triplet microtubules and fail to undergo centriole maturation.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by immunofluorescence data showing lack of maturation markers.

claim: Centrioles in epsilon-tubulin null mutant human cells fail to undergo centriole maturation.
source: Here, we report that centrioles in delta-tubulin and epsilon-tubulin null mutant human cells lack triplet microtubules and fail to undergo centriole maturation.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by immunofluorescence data showing lack of maturation markers.

claim: Aberrant centrioles in delta-tubulin and epsilon-tubulin null mutant cells are formed de novo each cell cycle.
source: These aberrant centrioles are formed de novo each cell cycle, but are unstable and do not persist to the next cell cycle, leading to a futile cycle of centriole formation and disintegration.
evidence: This is supported by cell cycle analysis and live imaging data showing centriole formation in S phase and loss in G1.

claim: Aberrant centrioles in delta-tubulin and epsilon-tubulin null mutant cells are unstable and do not persist to the next cell cycle.
source: These aberrant centrioles are formed de novo each cell cycle, but are unstable and do not persist to the next cell cycle, leading to a futile cycle of centriole formation and disintegration.
evidence: This is supported by time-course experiments and live imaging showing centriole disappearance after mitosis.

claim: Delta-tubulin and epsilon-tubulin null mutant cells undergo a futile cycle of centriole formation and disintegration.
source: These aberrant centrioles are formed de novo each cell cycle, but are unstable and do not persist to the next cell cycle, leading to a futile cycle of centriole formation and disintegration.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the data showing repeated formation in S phase and loss in G1.

claim: Centriole disintegration in delta-tubulin and epsilon-tubulin null mutant cells can be suppressed by paclitaxel treatment.
source: Disintegration can be suppressed by paclitaxel treatment.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data showing centriole persistence after paclitaxel treatment.

claim: Delta-tubulin and epsilon-tubulin physically interact.
source: Delta-tubulin and epsilon-tubulin physically interact, indicating that these tubulins act together to maintain triplet microtubules and that these are necessary for inheritance of centrioles from one cell cycle to the next.
evidence: This is supported by co-immunoprecipitation experiments shown in the manuscript.

claim: Triplet microtubules are necessary for inheritance of centrioles from one cell cycle to the next.
source: Delta-tubulin and epsilon-tubulin physically interact, indicating that these tubulins act together to maintain triplet microtubules and that these are necessary for inheritance of centrioles from one cell cycle to the next.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that centrioles lacking triplets do not persist to the next cell cycle.

claim: Centriolar microtubules have a triplet structure in most organisms, including humans.
source: In most organisms, including humans, the centriolar microtubules have a triplet structure, found only in centrioles.
evidence: This is established knowledge about centriole structure.

claim: The triplet structure consists of a complete A-tubule and associated partial B-tubule attached to the A-tubule wall, and a partial C-tubule attached to the B-tubule wall.
source: This structure consists of a complete A-tubule and associated partial B-tubule attached to the A-tubule wall, and a partial C-tubule attached to the B-tubule wall.
evidence: This is established knowledge about the structure of triplet microtubules.

claim: The molecular mechanisms involved in making triplet microtubules are not well-understood in mammalian cells.
source: The molecular mechanisms involved in making triplet microtubules are not well-understood, even in the well-characterized somatic centriole cycle of mammalian cells.
evidence: This is a statement about the state of knowledge in the field.

claim: Centrioles duplicate once per cycle in mammalian somatic cells.
source: In these cells centrioles duplicate once per cycle, such that daughter cells receive exactly one pair of centrioles.
evidence: This is established knowledge about the centriole duplication cycle.

claim: Centriole duplication is initiated at the G1-S transition when PLK4 localizes to a single focus on the mother centriole.
source: Centriole duplication is initiated at the G1-S transition when the kinase PLK4 localizes to a single focus on the mother centriole (Sonnen et al., 2012).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: The cartwheel, formed by SASS6 oligomerization, assembles to template the 9-fold symmetry of the newly-formed procentriole.
source: Subsequently, the cartwheel, formed by SASS6 oligomerization, assembles to template the 9-fold symmetry of the newly-formed procentriole (Guichard et al., 2017; Hilbert et al., 2016).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: Microtubules are added to the cartwheel underneath a cap of CP110.
source: Microtubules are added to the cartwheel underneath a cap of CP110 (Kleylein-Sohn et al., 2007).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: By G2-M, the triplet microtubules are completely formed.
source: By G2-M, the triplet microtubules are completely formed (Vorobjev and Chentsov YuS, 1982).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: The A- and B-tubules elongate to the full ~500 nm length of the centriole, forming a distal compartment with doublet microtubules marked by POC5.
source: Subsequently, the A- and B-tubules elongate to the full ~500 nm length of the centriole, forming a distal compartment with doublet microtubules and marked by POC5 (Azimzadeh et al., 2009).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: In mitosis, the cartwheel is lost.
source: In mitosis, the cartwheel is lost, and the newly-formed centriole becomes disengaged from its mother and acquires pericentriolar material (Vorobjev and Chentsov, 1980; Vorobjev and Chentsov YuS, 1982; Khodjakov and Rieder, 1999; Tsou and Stearns, 2006; Tsou et al., 2009).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: The newly-formed centriole becomes disengaged from its mother in mitosis.
source: In mitosis, the cartwheel is lost, and the newly-formed centriole becomes disengaged from its mother and acquires pericentriolar material (Vorobjev and Chentsov, 1980; Vorobjev and Chentsov YuS, 1982; Khodjakov and Rieder, 1999; Tsou and Stearns, 2006; Tsou et al., 2009).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: The newly-formed centriole acquires pericentriolar material in mitosis.
source: In mitosis, the cartwheel is lost, and the newly-formed centriole becomes disengaged from its mother and acquires pericentriolar material (Vorobjev and Chentsov, 1980; Vorobjev and Chentsov YuS, 1982; Khodjakov and Rieder, 1999; Tsou and Stearns, 2006; Tsou et al., 2009).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: In G2-M of the following cell cycle, the centriole acquires appendages, marking its maturation into a centriole that can nucleate a cilium.
source: In G2-M of the following cell cycle, the centriole acquires appendages, marking its maturation into a centriole that can nucleate a cilium (Graser et al., 2007; Guarguaglini et al., 2005).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: All eukaryotes have alpha-, beta- and gamma-tubulin.
source: All eukaryotes have alpha-, beta- and gamma-tubulin, but the tubulin superfamily also includes three less-studied members, delta-tubulin, epsilon-tubulin, and zeta-tubulin.
evidence: This is established knowledge about tubulin distribution across eukaryotes.

claim: The tubulin superfamily includes delta-tubulin, epsilon-tubulin, and zeta-tubulin.
source: All eukaryotes have alpha-, beta- and gamma-tubulin, but the tubulin superfamily also includes three less-studied members, delta-tubulin, epsilon-tubulin, and zeta-tubulin.
evidence: This is established knowledge about the tubulin superfamily.

claim: Delta-tubulin, epsilon-tubulin, and zeta-tubulin are found in a subset of eukaryotes and are evolutionarily co-conserved, making up the ZED tubulin module.
source: These tubulins are found in a subset of eukaryotes, and are evolutionarily co-conserved, making up the ZED tubulin module (Turk et al., 2015).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: In Chlamydomonas, mutations in delta-tubulin or epsilon-tubulin result in centrioles that lack triplet microtubules.
source: In the unicellular eukaryotes Chlamydomonas, Tetrahymena, Paramecium and Trypanosoma, mutations in delta-tubulin or epsilon-tubulin result in centrioles that lack triplet microtubules (Dupuis-Williams et al., 2002; Dutcher and Trabuco, 1998; Dutcher et al., 2002; Gadelha et al., 2006; Garreau de Loubresse et al., 2001; Goodenough and StClair, 1975; Ross et al., 2013).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: In Tetrahymena, mutations in delta-tubulin or epsilon-tubulin result in centrioles that lack triplet microtubules.
source: In the unicellular eukaryotes Chlamydomonas, Tetrahymena, Paramecium and Trypanosoma, mutations in delta-tubulin or epsilon-tubulin result in centrioles that lack triplet microtubules (Dupuis-Williams et al., 2002; Dutcher and Trabuco, 1998; Dutcher et al., 2002; Gadelha et al., 2006; Garreau de Loubresse et al., 2001; Goodenough and StClair, 1975; Ross et al., 2013).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: In Paramecium, mutations in delta-tubulin or epsilon-tubulin result in centrioles that lack triplet microtubules.
source: In the unicellular eukaryotes Chlamydomonas, Tetrahymena, Paramecium and Trypanosoma, mutations in delta-tubulin or epsilon-tubulin result in centrioles that lack triplet microtubules (Dupuis-Williams et al., 2002; Dutcher and Trabuco, 1998; Dutcher et al., 2002; Gadelha et al., 2006; Garreau de Loubresse et al., 2001; Goodenough and StClair, 1975; Ross et al., 2013).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: In Trypanosoma, mutations in delta-tubulin or epsilon-tubulin result in centrioles that lack triplet microtubules.
source: In the unicellular eukaryotes Chlamydomonas, Tetrahymena, Paramecium and Trypanosoma, mutations in delta-tubulin or epsilon-tubulin result in centrioles that lack triplet microtubules (Dupuis-Williams et al., 2002; Dutcher and Trabuco, 1998; Dutcher et al., 2002; Gadelha et al., 2006; Garreau de Loubresse et al., 2001; Goodenough and StClair, 1975; Ross et al., 2013).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: Humans and other placental mammals have delta-tubulin and epsilon-tubulin, but lack zeta-tubulin.
source: Humans and other placental mammals have delta-tubulin and epsilon-tubulin, but lack zeta-tubulin (Findeisen et al., 2014; Turk et al., 2015).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: Loss of centrioles in mammalian cells results in a p53-dependent cell-cycle arrest.
source: Recent work has established that loss of centrioles in mammalian cells results in a p53-dependent cell-cycle arrest (Bazzi and Anderson, 2014; Lambrus et al., 2015; Wong et al., 2015).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: Homozygous null mutations of delta-tubulin or epsilon-tubulin could only be isolated in TP53−/− cells.
source: We found that homozygous null mutations of delta-tubulin or epsilon-tubulin could only be isolated in TP53−/− cells, thus all subsequent experiments use RPE-1 TP53−/− cells as the control.
evidence: This is an experimental observation from the study.

claim: Three TUBD1−/− cell lines were generated.
source: Three TUBD1−/− and two TUBE1−/− cell lines were generated (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is a description of the experimental materials generated.

claim: Two TUBE1−/− cell lines were generated.
source: Three TUBD1−/− and two TUBE1−/− cell lines were generated (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is a description of the experimental materials generated.

claim: The TUBD1−/− lines are all compound heterozygotes bearing small deletions of less than 20 base pairs proximal to the cut site on one chromosome and insertion of one base pair on the other, resulting in frameshift and premature stop mutations.
source: The TUBD1−/− lines are all compound heterozygotes bearing small deletions of less than 20 base pairs proximal to the cut site on one chromosome and insertion of one base pair on the other, resulting in frameshift and premature stop mutations.
evidence: This is based on sequencing data of the mutant alleles.

claim: The two TUBE1−/− lines are compound heterozygotes bearing large deletions surrounding the cut site, that in each case remove an entire exon and surrounding DNA, including the ATG start site.
source: The two TUBE1−/− lines are also compound heterozygotes bearing large deletions surrounding the cut site, that in each case remove an entire exon and surrounding DNA, including the ATG start site.
evidence: This is based on sequencing data of the mutant alleles.

claim: Many TUBD1−/− and TUBE1−/− cells in an asynchronous population had multiple, unpaired centrin foci.
source: Many cells in an asynchronous population had multiple, unpaired centrin foci (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is an observation from immunofluorescence microscopy.

claim: The centrin foci in TUBD1−/− and TUBE1−/− cells also labeled with the centriolar proteins CP110 and SASS6.
source: These foci also labeled with the centriolar proteins CP110 and SASS6 (see Figures 2 and 3).
evidence: This is an observation from immunofluorescence microscopy.

claim: Some of the centrin-positive foci in TUBE1−/− cells corresponded to structures that resemble centrioles, but were narrower than typical centrioles and lack appendages.
source: In serial sections of interphase TUBE1−/− (Figure 1A) and TUBD1−/− (Figure 1B) cells, some of the centrin-positive foci corresponded to structures that resemble centrioles, but were narrower than typical centrioles and lack appendages.
evidence: This is an observation from correlative light-electron microscopy shown in Figure 1A.

claim: Some of the centrin-positive foci in TUBD1−/− cells corresponded to structures that resemble centrioles, but were narrower than typical centrioles and lack appendages.
source: In serial sections of interphase TUBE1−/− (Figure 1A) and TUBD1−/− (Figure 1B) cells, some of the centrin-positive foci corresponded to structures that resemble centrioles, but were narrower than typical centrioles and lack appendages.
evidence: This is an observation from correlative light-electron microscopy shown in Figure 1B.

claim: Only singlet microtubules were identified in the two centriole cross-sections observed from TUBD1−/− cells.
source: Strikingly, only singlet microtubules were identified in the two centriole cross-sections observed, both from TUBD1−/− cells (Figure 1C).
evidence: This is an observation from electron microscopy shown in Figure 1C.

claim: Centrioles in TUBD1−/− cells had an outer diameter of 172.5 nm ±13 nm (n = 17).
source: Centrioles in TUBD1−/− and TUBE1−/− cells were of similar outer diameter: 172.5 nm ±13 nm in TUBD1−/− cells (n = 17), 174.6 nm ±8 nm in TUBE1−/− cells (n = 13).
evidence: This is a quantitative measurement from electron microscopy data.

claim: Centrioles in TUBE1−/− cells had an outer diameter of 174.6 nm ±8 nm (n = 13).
source: Centrioles in TUBD1−/− and TUBE1−/− cells were of similar outer diameter: 172.5 nm ±13 nm in TUBD1−/− cells (n = 17), 174.6 nm ±8 nm in TUBE1−/− cells (n = 13).
evidence: This is a quantitative measurement from electron microscopy data.

claim: Mother centrioles in control TP53−/− cells had an outer diameter of 222.9 ± 9 nm (n = 24).
source: In contrast, centrioles in control TP53−/− cells had a larger diameter: 222.9 ± 9 nm (n = 24) for mother centrioles, and 212.1 ± 10 nm (n = 10) for procentrioles, similar to previous measurements of mammalian cell centrioles (Loncarek et al., 2008; Wang et al., 2015).
evidence: This is a quantitative measurement from electron microscopy data, consistent with prior literature.

claim: Procentrioles in control TP53−/− cells had an outer diameter of 212.1 ± 10 nm (n = 10).
source: In contrast, centrioles in control TP53−/− cells had a larger diameter: 222.9 ± 9 nm (n = 24) for mother centrioles, and 212.1 ± 10 nm (n = 10) for procentrioles, similar to previous measurements of mammalian cell centrioles (Loncarek et al., 2008; Wang et al., 2015).
evidence: This is a quantitative measurement from electron microscopy data, consistent with prior literature.

claim: The reduced outer diameter of aberrant centrioles in TUBD1−/− and TUBE1−/− cells is consistent with the presence of only singlet microtubules.
source: The reduced outer diameter of these aberrant centrioles is consistent with the presence of only singlet microtubules (Vorobjev and Chentsov YuS, 1982).
evidence: This is an inference based on the diameter measurements and comparison to prior literature.

claim: Mutant centrioles in TUBD1−/− and TUBE1−/− cells have a slightly reduced central lumen diameter.
source: We also noted that there is a slightly reduced central lumen diameter in mutant centrioles (Figure 1E).
evidence: This is an observation from electron microscopy measurements shown in Figure 1E.

claim: Normal procentrioles with singlet microtubules, prior to the elaboration of triplets, have a reduced lumenal diameter.
source: It is less clear why the mutant centrioles would have a reduced lumenal diameter, but we note that this result is consistent with the observation that normal procentrioles with singlet microtubules, prior to the elaboration of triplets, also have a reduced lumenal diameter (Vorobjev and Chentsov YuS, 1982).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: The length of centrioles from TUBD1−/− cells in interphase was 222 nm ±37 nm (n = 18).
source: In interphase, the length of centrioles from TUBD1−/− cells (222 nm ±37 nm; n = 18) and TUBE1−/− cells (339 nm ±131 nm; n = 15) was similar to that of control procentrioles (207 nm ±20 nm; n = 9) (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is a quantitative measurement from electron microscopy data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: The length of centrioles from TUBE1−/− cells in interphase was 339 nm ±131 nm (n = 15).
source: In interphase, the length of centrioles from TUBD1−/− cells (222 nm ±37 nm; n = 18) and TUBE1−/− cells (339 nm ±131 nm; n = 15) was similar to that of control procentrioles (207 nm ±20 nm; n = 9) (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is a quantitative measurement from electron microscopy data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: The length of control procentrioles in interphase was 207 nm ±20 nm (n = 9).
source: In interphase, the length of centrioles from TUBD1−/− cells (222 nm ±37 nm; n = 18) and TUBE1−/− cells (339 nm ±131 nm; n = 15) was similar to that of control procentrioles (207 nm ±20 nm; n = 9) (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is a quantitative measurement from electron microscopy data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: Control mother centrioles had a length of 485.6 nm ±43 nm (n = 14).
source: All were shorter than control mother centrioles (485.6 nm ±43 nm; n = 14).
evidence: This is a quantitative measurement from electron microscopy data.

claim: Centrioles in a TUBE1−/− prometaphase cell exhibited a morphological phenotype consisting of two electron-dense segments, one of ~50 nm and the other of ~200 nm, connected by singlet microtubules spanning a gap of ~250 nm.
source: These centrioles (n = 3) exhibited a remarkable morphological phenotype, consisting of two electron-dense segments, one of ~50 nm and the other of ~200 nm, connected by singlet microtubules spanning a gap of ~250 nm.
evidence: This is an observation from correlative light-electron microscopy shown in Figure 2B.

claim: The combined length of the two electron-dense segments and gap in TUBE1−/− prometaphase centrioles (~500 nm) approximates that of typical mature mammalian centrioles.
source: The combined length (~500 nm) of these structures approximates that of typical mature mammalian centrioles (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is an observation from electron microscopy measurements shown in Figure 2A.

claim: Procentrioles in control cells reached a full length of 403 nm ±22 nm in G2-M.
source: Procentrioles in control cells reached a full length of 403 nm ±22 nm in G2-M (Figure 2A), an increase of approximately 200 nm from their interphase state.
evidence: This is a quantitative measurement from electron microscopy data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: In TUBD1−/−, TUBE1−/−, and control interphase cells, the centroids of CP110 and SASS6 foci were separated by a mean distance of 0.3 μm.
source: We found that in TUBD1−/− and TUBE1−/− and control interphase cells, the centroids of CP110 and SASS6 foci were separated by a mean distance of 0.3 μm, whereas in mitotic cells the foci were separated by a mean distance of 0.5 μm (Figure 2C,D).
evidence: This is a quantitative measurement from immunofluorescence microscopy shown in Figure 2C,D.

claim: In TUBD1−/−, TUBE1−/−, and control mitotic cells, the centroids of CP110 and SASS6 foci were separated by a mean distance of 0.5 μm.
source: We found that in TUBD1−/− and TUBE1−/− and control interphase cells, the centroids of CP110 and SASS6 foci were separated by a mean distance of 0.3 μm, whereas in mitotic cells the foci were separated by a mean distance of 0.5 μm (Figure 2C,D).
evidence: This is a quantitative measurement from immunofluorescence microscopy shown in Figure 2C,D.

claim: Centrioles in TUBD1−/− and TUBE1−/− cells undergo normal cell cycle-dependent elongation.
source: Thus, despite their structural defects, centrioles in TUBD1−/− and TUBE1−/− cells undergo the normal cell cycle-dependent elongation.
evidence: This is inferred from the CP110-SASS6 separation measurements.

claim: The distal compartment of mammalian centrioles is defined by the centrin-binding protein POC5.
source: In mammalian cells this compartment is defined by the centrin-binding protein POC5 (Azimzadeh et al., 2009).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: POC5 was present in centrioles from mitotic control cells.
source: Consistent with this, we found that POC5 was present in centrioles from mitotic control cells and absent from those in TUBD1−/− and TUBE1−/− cells (Figure 2E).
evidence: This is an observation from immunofluorescence microscopy shown in Figure 2E.

claim: POC5 was absent from centrioles in mitotic TUBD1−/− and TUBE1−/− cells.
source: Consistent with this, we found that POC5 was present in centrioles from mitotic control cells and absent from those in TUBD1−/− and TUBE1−/− cells (Figure 2E).
evidence: This is an observation from immunofluorescence microscopy shown in Figure 2E.

claim: The doublet microtubules of the extended centriole distal end are required for defining the distal compartment.
source: This suggests that the doublet microtubules of the extended centriole distal end are required for defining this compartment.
evidence: This is inferred from the absence of POC5 in mutant centrioles that lack doublet microtubules.

claim: Control cells had approximately 50% of cells having two centrioles, corresponding to cells in G1 phase.
source: Control cells had a centriole number distribution typical of TP53−/− cells, with approximately 50% of cells having two centrioles, corresponding to cells in G1 phase, 40% having three to four centrioles, corresponding to cells in S through M phases, and 10% having more than four centrioles (Figure 3A,B).
evidence: This is an observation from immunofluorescence microscopy shown in Figure 3A,B.

claim: Control cells had approximately 40% having three to four centrioles, corresponding to cells in S through M phases.
source: Control cells had a centriole number distribution typical of TP53−/− cells, with approximately 50% of cells having two centrioles, corresponding to cells in G1 phase, 40% having three to four centrioles, corresponding to cells in S through M phases, and 10% having more than four centrioles (Figure 3A,B).
evidence: This is an observation from immunofluorescence microscopy shown in Figure 3A,B.

claim: Control cells had approximately 10% having more than four centrioles.
source: Control cells had a centriole number distribution typical of TP53−/− cells, with approximately 50% of cells having two centrioles, corresponding to cells in G1 phase, 40% having three to four centrioles, corresponding to cells in S through M phases, and 10% having more than four centrioles (Figure 3A,B).
evidence: This is an observation from immunofluorescence microscopy shown in Figure 3A,B.

claim: In TUBD1−/− and TUBE1−/− cells, approximately 50% of cells had five or more centriole foci.
source: In contrast, in TUBD1−/− and TUBE1−/− cells, approximately 50% of cells had five or more centriole foci, whereas 50% of cells had no detectable centriole foci (Figure 3A,B).
evidence: This is an observation from immunofluorescence microscopy shown in Figure 3A,B.

claim: In TUBD1−/− and TUBE1−/− cells, approximately 50% of cells had no detectable centriole foci.
source: In contrast, in TUBD1−/− and TUBE1−/− cells, approximately 50% of cells had five or more centriole foci, whereas 50% of cells had no detectable centriole foci (Figure 3A,B).
evidence: This is an observation from immunofluorescence microscopy shown in Figure 3A,B.

claim: The centriole phenotype in TUBD1−/− and TUBE1−/− cells could be rescued by expression of delta-tubulin and epsilon-tubulin, respectively.
source: Similar centriole distributions were found in several independently derived TUBD1−/− and TUBE1−/− cell lines, and this phenotype could be rescued by expression of delta-tubulin and epsilon-tubulin, respectively (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A,B).
evidence: This is an observation from rescue experiments shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1A,B.

claim: The centrioles in TUBD1−/− and TUBE1−/− cells were never observed to be closely apposed, as is typical of wild-type cells.
source: In agreement with this hypothesis, the centrioles in mutant cells, as visualized by centrin and CP110 were never observed to be closely apposed, as is typical of wild-type cells (Figure 3A).
evidence: This is an observation from immunofluorescence microscopy shown in Figure 3A.

claim: The centrioles in asynchronous TUBD1−/− and TUBE1−/− cells all lacked Cep164.
source: The centrioles in asynchronous TUBD1−/− and TUBE1−/− cells all lacked Cep164, a component of the centriolar distal appendage and marker of mature centrioles that have progressed through at least one cell cycle (Figure 3C), whereas approximately 40% of all centrioles were positive for Cep164 in asynchronous control cells, consistent with the cycle of distal appendage acquisition (Nigg and Stearns, 2011).
evidence: This is an observation from immunofluorescence microscopy shown in Figure 3C.

claim: Approximately 40% of all centrioles were positive for Cep164 in asynchronous control cells.
source: The centrioles in asynchronous TUBD1−/− and TUBE1−/− cells all lacked Cep164, a component of the centriolar distal appendage and marker of mature centrioles that have progressed through at least one cell cycle (Figure 3C), whereas approximately 40% of all centrioles were positive for Cep164 in asynchronous control cells, consistent with the cycle of distal appendage acquisition (Nigg and Stearns, 2011).
evidence: This is an observation from immunofluorescence microscopy shown in Figure 3C.

claim: Most of the centrioles in TUBD1−/− and TUBE1−/− cells lacked detectable gamma-tubulin.
source: Lastly, most of the centrioles in TUBD1−/− and TUBE1−/− cells lacked detectable gamma-tubulin (Figure 3C), and those that stained positive had less than centrioles in control cells (Figure 3—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is an observation from immunofluorescence microscopy shown in Figure 3C.

claim: SASS6 was present in most of the centrioles in TUBD1−/− and TUBE1−/− cells.
source: In addition, we noted that SASS6, the cartwheel protein that is present in nascent and recently-formed centrioles, but is lost from centrioles at the mitosis-interphase transition in human cells, was present in most of the centrioles in TUBD1−/− and TUBE1−/− cells, consistent with these centrioles originating in the observed cell cycle, but not having successfully persisted into the subsequent cell cycle.
evidence: This is an observation from immunofluorescence microscopy.

claim: TUBD1−/− and TUBE1−/− cells in G0/G1 mostly lacked centriole structures.
source: TUBD1−/− and TUBE1−/− cells in G0/G1 mostly lacked centriole structures, whereas cells in S-phase, G2 and mitosis had them.
evidence: This is an observation from cell cycle-staged immunofluorescence microscopy shown in Figure 3D.

claim: TUBD1−/− and TUBE1−/− cells in S-phase, G2 and mitosis had centriole structures.
source: TUBD1−/− and TUBE1−/− cells in G0/G1 mostly lacked centriole structures, whereas cells in S-phase, G2 and mitosis had them.
evidence: This is an observation from cell cycle-staged immunofluorescence microscopy shown in Figure 3D.

claim: In TUBD1−/− and TUBE1−/− cells, aberrant centrioles are formed in S-phase, persist into mitosis, and are absent in G1.
source: These results indicate that in TUBD1−/− and TUBE1−/− cells, aberrant centrioles are formed in S-phase, persist into mitosis, and are absent in G1.
evidence: This is inferred from the cell cycle-staged observations.

claim: The loss of centriole structure in TUBD1−/− and TUBE1−/− cells is likely due to a specific event that occurs at the mitosis-interphase transition, rather than simply time since formation.
source: We note that this loss of centriole structure is likely due to a specific event that occurs at the mitosis-interphase transition, rather than simply time since formation, since cells were arrested in G2 for 24 hr, which is substantially longer than the normal progression through mitosis to G1, nevertheless the centriole structures persisted (Figure 3D).
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that centrioles persist during prolonged G2 arrest but are lost after mitosis.

claim: In control cells, the number of centrioles followed the pattern expected from the centriole duplication cycle.
source: In control cells, the number of centrioles followed the pattern expected from the centriole duplication cycle.
evidence: This is an observation from time-course experiments shown in Figure 3E.

claim: In TUBE1−/− cells, the majority of mitotic cells had centrioles.
source: In TUBE1−/− cells, the majority of mitotic cells had centrioles.
evidence: This is an observation from time-course experiments shown in Figure 3E.

claim: By 1 hr after mitotic shakeoff, the fraction of interphase TUBE1−/− cells without centrioles had increased to 50%.
source: By 1 hr after shakeoff, the fraction of interphase cells without centrioles had increased to 50%, and this fraction continued to increase at 2 hr and 3 hr after shakeoff.
evidence: This is an observation from time-course experiments shown in Figure 3E.

claim: By 12 hr after mitotic shakeoff, 56 ± 12% of TUBE1−/− cells had entered S-phase, and centriole structures began to appear.
source: By 12 hr after shakeoff, 56 ± 12% of cells had entered S-phase, and centriole structures began to appear, consistent with de novo centriole formation.
evidence: This is an observation from time-course experiments shown in Figure 3E.

claim: Centrioles in control cells segregated normally in mitosis.
source: Centrioles in control cells segregated normally in mitosis, and the mitotic interval was 46 min ±6 min (n = 11).
evidence: This is an observation from live cell imaging shown in Figure 3F and Video 1.

claim: The mitotic interval in control cells was 46 min ±6 min (n = 11).
source: Centrioles in control cells segregated normally in mitosis, and the mitotic interval was 46 min ±6 min (n = 11).
evidence: This is a quantitative measurement from live cell imaging shown in Figure 3F and Video 1.

claim: Centrioles in TUBE1−/− cells did not persist into the next interphase.
source: In contrast, centrioles in TUBE1−/− cells did not persist into the next interphase, and the mitotic interval was longer, at 106 min ±43 min (n = 10).
evidence: This is an observation from live cell imaging shown in Figure 3F and Video 2.

claim: The mitotic interval in TUBE1−/− cells was 106 min ±43 min (n = 10).
source: In contrast, centrioles in TUBE1−/− cells did not persist into the next interphase, and the mitotic interval was longer, at 106 min ±43 min (n = 10).
evidence: This is a quantitative measurement from live cell imaging shown in Figure 3F and Video 2.

claim: The prolonged time in mitosis in TUBE1−/− cells is similar to that observed for acentriolar human cells.
source: The prolonged time in mitosis is similar to that observed for acentriolar human cells (Lambrus et al., 2015).
evidence: This is a comparison to prior literature.

claim: Delta-tubulin and epsilon-tubulin are not required to initiate centriole formation in human cells.
source: Thus, delta-tubulin and epsilon-tubulin are not required to initiate centriole formation in human cells, but the aberrant centrioles that form in their absence are unstable and disintegrate during progression from M phase to the subsequent G1 phase.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that centrioles form in mutant cells but are unstable.

claim: De novo centrioles formed after washout of the centriole duplication inhibitor centrinone persisted through mitosis and the subsequent G1.
source: De novo centrioles formed after washout of the centriole duplication inhibitor centrinone persisted through mitosis and the subsequent G1 (Figure 3—figure supplement 1D), consistent with previous reports (La Terra et al., 2005).
evidence: This is an observation from centrinone washout experiments shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1D.

claim: Paclitaxel treatment did not prevent centriole elongation in TUBE1−/− cells.
source: Paclitaxel treatment did not prevent centriole elongation, as measured by the separation between CP110 and SASS6 foci, as in Figure 2 (0.49 µm ± 0.2 µm; n = 105; not significantly different from TUBE1−/− mitotic cells in Figure 2 by unpaired two-tailed t-test).
evidence: This is a quantitative measurement from immunofluorescence microscopy.

claim: Centrioles in TUBE1−/− cells were still present 3 hr after RO-3306 treatment when cells were pre-treated with paclitaxel.
source: Centrioles in these cells were still present 3 hr after RO-3306 treatment, whereas control RO-3306-treated cells that were not treated with paclitaxel lacked centrioles (Figure 4A,B).
evidence: This is an observation from drug treatment experiments shown in Figure 4A,B.

claim: Control RO-3306-treated TUBE1−/− cells that were not treated with paclitaxel lacked centrioles.
source: Centrioles in these cells were still present 3 hr after RO-3306 treatment, whereas control RO-3306-treated cells that were not treated with paclitaxel lacked centrioles (Figure 4A,B).
evidence: This is an observation from drug treatment experiments shown in Figure 4A,B.

claim: The TUBE1−/− centrioles stabilized by paclitaxel treatment still failed to recruit high levels of gamma-tubulin.
source: However, the TUBE1−/− centrioles stabilized by paclitaxel treatment still failed to recruit high levels of gamma-tubulin (Figure 4C), and lost their SASS6 cartwheel (97% ± 2% cells completely lack SASS6 foci, three independent experiments with 100 cells each; and Figure 4D) as expected for centrioles that have transited mitosis.
evidence: This is an observation from immunofluorescence microscopy shown in Figure 4C.

claim: The TUBE1−/− centrioles stabilized by paclitaxel treatment lost their SASS6 cartwheel (97% ± 2% cells completely lack SASS6 foci).
source: However, the TUBE1−/− centrioles stabilized by paclitaxel treatment still failed to recruit high levels of gamma-tubulin (Figure 4C), and lost their SASS6 cartwheel (97% ± 2% cells completely lack SASS6 foci, three independent experiments with 100 cells each; and Figure 4D) as expected for centrioles that have transited mitosis.
evidence: This is a quantitative observation from immunofluorescence microscopy shown in Figure 4D.

claim: Preventing depolymerization of the centriolar microtubules in TUBE1−/− cells stabilizes the structure of these aberrant centrioles such that they survive into the next cell cycle.
source: We propose that preventing depolymerization of the centriolar microtubules in TUBE1−/− cells stabilizes the structure of these aberrant centrioles such that they survive into the next cell cycle.
evidence: This is a proposed mechanism based on the paclitaxel rescue experiments.

claim: Epsilon-tubulin could be immunoprecipitated with delta-tubulin from human HEK293T cells.
source: Epsilon-tubulin could be immunoprecipitated with delta-tubulin, and not with GFP from control cells (Figure 4E).
evidence: This is an observation from co-immunoprecipitation experiments shown in Figure 4E.

claim: Epsilon-tubulin could not be immunoprecipitated with GFP from control cells.
source: Epsilon-tubulin could be immunoprecipitated with delta-tubulin, and not with GFP from control cells (Figure 4E).
evidence: This is an observation from co-immunoprecipitation experiments shown in Figure 4E.

claim: Delta-tubulin and epsilon-tubulin may dimerize to form higher-order structures, as do alpha-tubulin and beta-tubulin.
source: These results indicate that epsilon-tubulin and delta-tubulin can interact, and we speculate that they may dimerize to form higher-order structures, as do alpha-tubulin and beta-tubulin.
evidence: This is speculation based on the interaction data and comparison to alpha/beta-tubulin.

claim: The presence of triplet centriolar microtubules is not strictly correlated with the presence of delta-tubulin and epsilon-tubulin in evolution.
source: The former seems unlikely, since the presence of triplet centriolar microtubules is not strictly correlated with the presence of delta-tubulin and epsilon-tubulin in evolution (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is based on evolutionary analysis shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: C. elegans lacks delta-tubulin, epsilon-tubulin, and triplet microtubules.
source: Among the organisms that lack delta-tubulin and epsilon-tubulin, C. elegans lacks triplet microtubules, but both Drosophila and the plant Ginkgo biloba have triplet microtubules in their sperm cells.
evidence: This is established knowledge about C. elegans centriole structure.

claim: Drosophila lacks delta-tubulin and epsilon-tubulin but has triplet microtubules in sperm cells.
source: Among the organisms that lack delta-tubulin and epsilon-tubulin, C. elegans lacks triplet microtubules, but both Drosophila and the plant Ginkgo biloba have triplet microtubules in their sperm cells.
evidence: This is established knowledge about Drosophila centriole structure.

claim: Ginkgo biloba lacks delta-tubulin and epsilon-tubulin but has triplet microtubules in sperm cells.
source: Among the organisms that lack delta-tubulin and epsilon-tubulin, C. elegans lacks triplet microtubules, but both Drosophila and the plant Ginkgo biloba have triplet microtubules in their sperm cells.
evidence: This is established knowledge about Ginkgo biloba centriole structure.

claim: Triplet microtubule formation itself does not require delta-tubulin or epsilon-tubulin.
source: Since loss of these tubulins must have occurred independently in the dipteran insect and plant lineages, the most parsimonious interpretation is that triplet microtubule formation itself does not require delta-tubulin or epsilon-tubulin, rather than that these two lineages independently evolved mechanisms of triplet formation in their absence.
evidence: This is inferred from evolutionary analysis.

claim: Delta-tubulin and epsilon-tubulin are required for stabilization of the centriolar triplets in most organisms.
source: Thus, we consider it more likely that delta-tubulin and epsilon-tubulin are required for stabilization of the centriolar triplets in most organisms.
evidence: This is inferred from the evolutionary analysis and experimental data.

claim: Organisms that lack delta-tubulin and epsilon-tubulin have simpler centriole structures that lack typical distal appendages.
source: However, we note that those few centriole-bearing organisms that lack delta-tubulin and epsilon-tubulin have simpler centriole structures that lack typical distal appendages, and also often lack a distal compartment that is typical of more complex centrioles.
evidence: This is an observation from evolutionary analysis.

claim: Organisms that lack delta-tubulin and epsilon-tubulin often lack a distal compartment that is typical of more complex centrioles.
source: However, we note that those few centriole-bearing organisms that lack delta-tubulin and epsilon-tubulin have simpler centriole structures that lack typical distal appendages, and also often lack a distal compartment that is typical of more complex centrioles.
evidence: This is an observation from evolutionary analysis.

claim: Aberrant centrioles with elongated singlet microtubules in delta-tubulin and epsilon-tubulin mutant cells become unstable as cells progress through mitosis.
source: We have shown that in these cells, aberrant centrioles with elongated singlet microtubules become unstable as cells progress through mitosis, and that disintegration can be suppressed by treatment with the microtubule stabilizing drug paclitaxel.
evidence: This is a summary of the experimental findings.

claim: Ciliary axonemes made of doublet microtubules can be dynamic.
source: We note that ciliary axonemes, made of doublet microtubules, can be dynamic, although in Chlamydomonas, where this has been best characterized, disassembly of the axoneme is slow, and is under complex regulatory control (Lefebvre et al., 1978; Marshall et al., 2005; Hu et al., 2015).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: In Chlamydomonas, disassembly of the axoneme is slow and is under complex regulatory control.
source: We note that ciliary axonemes, made of doublet microtubules, can be dynamic, although in Chlamydomonas, where this has been best characterized, disassembly of the axoneme is slow, and is under complex regulatory control (Lefebvre et al., 1978; Marshall et al., 2005; Hu et al., 2015).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: Non-tubulin densities have been identified in cryoEM structures of centrioles and ciliary axonemes.
source: Consistent with this possibility, non-tubulin densities have been identified in cryoEM structures of centrioles and ciliary axonemes (Li et al., 2012; Ichikawa et al., 2017).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: POC5 is not recruited to singlet microtubule centrioles.
source: We found that POC5, a component of the distal end compartment, is not recruited to singlet microtubule centrioles; perhaps POC5 binds to and stabilizes the doublet microtubules in the distal compartment of centrioles.
evidence: This is an observation from the immunofluorescence experiments.

claim: POC5 may bind to and stabilize the doublet microtubules in the distal compartment of centrioles.
source: We found that POC5, a component of the distal end compartment, is not recruited to singlet microtubule centrioles; perhaps POC5 binds to and stabilizes the doublet microtubules in the distal compartment of centrioles.
evidence: This is speculation based on the observation that POC5 is not recruited to singlet microtubule centrioles.

claim: The poc1 mutant in Tetrahymena causes partial loss of the A-C linker and defects in triplet microtubule organization.
source: No components of the A-C linker have been identified, but the poc1 mutant in Tetrahymena causes partial loss of this linker and defects in triplet microtubule organization (Meehl et al., 2016).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: Delta-tubulin and epsilon-tubulin likely work together in a critical aspect of centriole structure and function.
source: Here we have shown that delta-tubulin and epsilon-tubulin likely work together in a critical aspect of centriole structure and function, and that cells lacking either tubulin undergo a futile cycle of de novo centriole formation and disintegration.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on the experimental findings.

claim: In human cells, delta-tubulin and epsilon-tubulin act to stabilize centriole structures necessary for inheritance of centrioles from one cell cycle to the next.
source: Our results show that in human cells, delta-tubulin and epsilon-tubulin act to stabilize centriole structures necessary for inheritance of centrioles from one cell cycle to the next, perhaps by stabilizing the main structural feature of centrioles, the triplet microtubules.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on the experimental findings.

claim: Delta-tubulin and epsilon-tubulin may stabilize centriole structures by stabilizing the triplet microtubules.
source: Our results show that in human cells, delta-tubulin and epsilon-tubulin act to stabilize centriole structures necessary for inheritance of centrioles from one cell cycle to the next, perhaps by stabilizing the main structural feature of centrioles, the triplet microtubules.
evidence: This is a proposed mechanism based on the experimental findings.
